common_name: Silver Greenheart Rex Begonia (Heirloom Green-Centered Silver Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; if summering outdoors, keep in a sheltered shady spot and bring back inside well before nighttime temperatures drop toward 50F.

directions: Pot in a light, well-drained mix and place where the plant gets bright, filtered light but no direct sun, which scorches the thin patterned leaves. Silver Greenheart is a long-grown Rex begonia heirloom prized for its broad silver leaf blade surrounding a contrasting deep-green heart-shaped center zone near the petiole, giving strong two-tone color from across a room. Keep humidity elevated with a pebble tray or grouping of plants, and let the topsoil dry slightly between waterings to avoid rhizome rot. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-wedge cuttings when repotting in spring.

common_name: Harmony's Hot Chocolate Rex Begonia (Deep Maroon-Brown Silver-Spotted Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Best grown as a year-round houseplant in bright, indirect light; only move outdoors in summer to a fully shaded, wind-protected spot once nights stay reliably above 50F.

directions: Site this cultivar in bright, indirect light and use a chunky, fast-draining potting mix, since the compact rhizome is prone to rot if kept wet. Harmony's Hot Chocolate belongs to the Harmony breeding series of Rex begonias and carries deep chocolate-maroon leaves overlaid with a metallic silver band, producing especially rich color under bright but sun-free conditions. Water only once the surface inch of mix has dried and maintain higher-than-average household humidity to keep leaf edges from crisping. Increase stock by dividing the rhizome or rooting a leaf-wedge cutting in a warm, humid propagation tray.

common_name: Grey Heart Rex Begonia (Silver-Grey Dark-Centered Pointed-Leaf Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Keep as an indoor foliage plant year-round in bright, indirect light; a shaded porch or patio is fine for summer once overnight temperatures are consistently above 50F.

directions: Grow Grey Heart in a peaty, well-aerated mix under bright, indirect light, turning the pot occasionally so the pointed leaves develop evenly on all sides. This cultivar is named for its smoky silver-grey leaf surface set off by a dark, near-black heart-shaped zone at the leaf base, a striking pattern that intensifies with consistent bright light. Water thoroughly and then let the mix approach dryness before watering again, since constantly soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome and root rot. Divide congested rhizomes in spring to refresh the plant and create new starts.

common_name: Great American Rex Begonia (Classic Large-Leaf Silver-and-Rose Banded Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Treat as a permanent houseplant grown in bright, indirect light year-round; it can spend summer outdoors in deep shade once nights are reliably above 50F.

directions: Provide bright, curtain-filtered light and a loose, humus-rich mix, since Great American is a vigorous older Rex cultivar that rewards good growing conditions with unusually large leaves. Its foliage carries broad concentric bands of silver, rose-pink, and deep green radiating out from the petiole, making it a longtime favorite among heirloom Rex begonia collectors. Water when the top of the mix feels dry and avoid letting water sit on the leaves, which can cause spotting. Refresh crowded plants by dividing the rhizome at repotting time in spring.

common_name: Purple Petticoats Rex Begonia (Ruffled Purple-Black Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow as a year-round indoor foliage plant in bright, indirect light; move to sheltered outdoor shade in summer only after nights stay above 50F.

directions: Place Purple Petticoats where it receives bright, indirect light and pot it in a fast-draining, aerated mix that lets excess moisture escape from the shallow rhizome. The cultivar takes its name from its deeply ruffled, wavy-margined leaves in dark purple-black tones, a dramatic contrast plant for mixed shade-loving foliage displays. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the surface to dry between waterings, and keep humidity elevated to prevent leaf-edge browning. New plants are easily started from rhizome divisions or leaf-wedge cuttings taken in spring.

common_name: Fairy Rex Begonia (Pink-Speckled Silver Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Keep indoors year-round in bright, indirect light; a shaded summer spot outdoors is acceptable once overnight lows stay above 50F.

directions: Fairy stays smaller than many Rex cultivars, so a shallow pot in bright, filtered light with a light, well-drained mix suits it well. Its green leaf surface is dusted with fine silvery-pink speckling that gives the whole plant a soft, frosted look rather than the bold banding seen in larger-leaved cultivars. Let the mix dry slightly at the surface between waterings and avoid cold drafts, which can stall growth. Divide the compact rhizome only when the pot becomes crowded, since this cultivar resents excessive disturbance.

common_name: Salamander Rex Begonia (Elongated Metallic-Sheen Pointed-Leaf Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow as a permanent houseplant in bright, indirect light; summer outdoors only in deep, wind-sheltered shade once nights are reliably above 50F.

directions: Salamander produces narrow, elongated, pointed leaves with a metallic silver sheen and dark contrasting veins, so place it where its slightly pendant foliage can be viewed from the side. Grow in bright, indirect light and a well-drained, humus-rich mix, watering only after the top inch of soil has dried to keep the shallow rhizome from rotting. Because its leaf shape and shine differ from the rounder, matte-textured Rex cultivars, it pairs well as a textural contrast in mixed shade-plant displays. Propagate by dividing the rhizome or rooting leaf-wedge cuttings in warm, humid conditions.

common_name: Comtesse Louise Erdody Rex Begonia (Heirloom Silver-Spotted Wavy-Edge Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow year-round as a houseplant in bright, indirect light; can be moved to a fully shaded outdoor spot for summer once nights stay above 50F.

directions: One of the oldest named Rex begonia cultivars still in cultivation, Comtesse Louise Erdody dates to the late nineteenth century and remains popular with heirloom collectors for its silver-spotted, gently wavy-edged leaves. Grow it in bright, indirect light and a light, well-aerated potting mix, keeping the plant out of direct sun to prevent the thin leaf surface from scorching. Water thoroughly and then allow the mix to dry slightly before the next watering, and maintain elevated humidity to keep the ruffled leaf margins from browning. Propagate by rhizome division at repotting time or from leaf-wedge cuttings.

common_name: Red Kiss Rex Begonia (Compact Pink-and-Red Center Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Grow indoors year-round in bright, indirect light as a compact houseplant; only move outdoors to full shade in summer once nights stay above 50F.

directions: Red Kiss is a compact, widely distributed Rex hybrid commonly sold as a flowering-aisle houseplant, with a vivid pink-to-red central leaf zone that fades outward to green edges. Grow it in bright, indirect light in a small pot with a fast-draining mix, since its dense root system and shallow rhizome are quick to rot if kept constantly wet. Allow the surface of the mix to dry between waterings and provide extra humidity indoors during winter heating season to keep leaf edges from crisping. Because it stays compact, it suits windowsills and terrarium-style displays better than larger, sprawling Rex cultivars.
